chunk_findings.detail: `window_start` computes the standing-window anchor from every ask row with a non-empty `policy` field, without restricting that set to rules currently enabled in `[approvals].policy` or to rows whose verb is in `[approvals].standing_verbs`. Thus an old policy answer from a disabled, removed, or out-of-scope rule controls `_window_open`. For example, if `skip_after_unavailable` auto-approved at `t=0` and was later disabled, then enabling `complete_unavailable` with `standing_verbs=["complete.force"]` and `standing_window_s=3600` sees `window_start() == 0.0` for the first `complete.force` at `t=7200`, so `_window_open` returns false and the request is person-only even though no in-scope standing rule has fired. Conversely, if the disabled rule fired at `t=7000`, the first `complete.force` at `t=7100` is auto-approved and the window closes at `t=10600`, 3600 seconds after the unrelated old answer rather than after the first complete-force standing approval. This violates the stated behavior that the first in-scope standing auto-approval opens the full configured window.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/approvals/policy.py:window_start

chunk_findings.detail: The test advances the clock by `cfg.approvals.standing_window_s + 1`, but the documented defaults make `standing_window_s` and the pre-existing `approvals.use_ttl_s` both 3600. Thus the assertion can pass for the wrong reason: if `operator_gate` persists `window_start` (so the first test passes) but still decides expiry only from the old per-answer TTL/count logic, then after 3601 seconds the TTL has also lapsed and `not after.ok` is true even though the new standing-window check is absent or inert. The test should set the two durations apart (for example `standing_window_s=60`, `use_ttl_s=3600`) and advance only past the window to prove the window, not the TTL, is what stops auto-approval.

chunk_findings.detail: The test reuses the same `canon` after the window lapses and only asserts `after.ask_id` and `"requested" in after.message`. It never captures the first auto-approved ask id or asserts that `after.ask_id` is a new, unanswered ask. If `operator_gate` returns the already answered ask id from the first policy approval together with its original “approval requested” message, the test still passes even though no new person ask was created, so it does not actually refute a stale-ask false positive.
